Sift Portals should link to randomly assorted pairs across dimensions. Currently, Nether portals link up to their cross-dimensional pair at the same coordinates but multiplied or divided by eight. This means you can use them to essentially travel 8x as fast across the Overworld. The End exit portal can be used to return to your spawn point when you enter from any of the naturally generating End entrance portals. I think there’s a perfect opportunity to give the Sift portals their own unique traversal behavior! It would be cool if Sift entrance portals linked up to exit portals at randomized coordinates. Then, if you can find a different naturally generating exit portal in the Sift, you can re-enter the Overworld at randomized coordinates! This could allow you to link up bases that are impossibly far away, which is completely impractical in the current game.

Salt Flats, Tar Pits, and Asphalt Salt Flats (or Salt Pans) are an environment I've always thought were pretty cool, and they'd make a great new Minecraft biome. Their vast expanses of flat whiteness would be a sight to behold and also make a great building location. So I thought I'd have a think about how they could be added to Minecraft, and it led me to Asphalt, a way of potentially improving non-elytra movement. (I threw the textures in these photos together in about 5 minutes, they're just meant to represent a rough visual guide and are no way something I'm proud of!) Salt Flats generate in areas of low humidity and low erosion, making them common near badlands and deserts. They are primarily composed of Salt, which lines the surface, and Hardened Salt, found below the surface. Salt is a soil-like block that is the sand or dirt of the Salt Flats. Walking on salt produces small salt-crystal-esque particle effects from the mob's feet, and it affected by gravity, similar to sand and gravel. Salt can be crafted into Salt Bricks (4 Salt in a 2-2 grid), which are decorative, gravity-affected brick blocks. Salt Bricks can be crafted into Salt Brick Slab, Stair, and Walls, giving us these gravity-affected variants. Salt and Salt Bricks (rough visual guide) Hardened Salt is the sandstone-equivalent of Salt, lining the bottom of the Salt Flats. It can be obtained by smelting Salt in a furnace, and are not affected by gravity. They can be crafted into Hardened Salt Bricks (4 Hardened Salt in a 2-2 grid), which have a Slab, Stair, and Wall variant, as well as Cracked Hardened Salt Bricks (via smelting Hardened Salt Bricks in a furnace) and Chiseled Hardened Salt Bricks, which are engraved with the face of Steve (or if the pale white eyes are to be considered, someone else entirely...) The Salt block sets on their own just present another white brick block set, and a flat, white biome. But within the Salt Flats generate Tar Pits, moderately-sized inky black depressions in the terrain that dot the otherwise pale white surface. Tar is a sticky block that generates naturally in Tar Pits in Salt Flats. It has a similar affect to honey, reducing the player's walk speed and jump height when in contact with the top block. Players can also slide down Tar like they can honey. Tar can be used as furnace fuel, with one block smelting four items, and it can be generated renewably in a similar way to lava; a Pointed Dripstone hanging from a Dripstone Block with Tar above it periodically produces tar drips. These drips have a 1/5 chance of turning water source blocks below the Pointed Dripstone into Tar. Tar can be crafted into Tar Bricks, (Slab, Stair, and Wall variant included), providing players with an inky black brick block set. But the mechanical benefits to Tar and Salt appear when you combined them together. Tar Asphalt is a block created by putting 2 Tar and 2 Salt in 2 by 2 formation in a crafting grid (produces 4 Asphalt). Asphalt has the interesting property of increasing mobs maximum speed and acceleration as they run along the surface of it. This property applies to players, but also ridden horses, pigs, camels, etc. As such, taking the time to lay out an Asphalt road would reward on-foot and horse transportation between two bases. Asphalt Now, I'm not super sure on the balancing behind the numbers, but I'm envisioning a max increase of about 4x when running along an Asphalt road. It needs to be an increase of enough to make laying out an Asphalt track between oft-frequented places worthwhile, but obviously not enough to break the game. Asphalt would increase acceleration and max run speed, though unlike on any other block, speed would be reduced if sprint-jumping, as you're making less contact with the top of the Asphalt block. You also obviously wouldn't be able to run on Asphalt when below 6 Hunger (and Asphalt Slabs would only increased max. speed/acceleration by 50% - no cheating the system there.) Obviously, Asphalt won't replace elytras, and it almost certainly wouldn't replace Nether Highways as a means of transportation. I don't think many suggestions posted in this sub will do that until the elytra 'issue' is addressed by Mojang itself. Instead, I imagine Asphalt supplementing horse and camel travel, by rewarding players who go out and find a Salt Flat and spend the time building an Asphalt road. That's the basis for Salt Flats, Tar Pits, and Asphalt. I'm open to any suggestions/discussion, this idea can definitely be improved. For example, I thought of maybe adding Road Runners as small ambient mobs that spawn in Salt Flats. Feed them seeds and they follow you around for ~10 minutes, and they mirror your movement speed, so you can run along Asphalt roads with them and they match your pace! I also tried to rack my brains thinking of ways Salt could act when in water, as very salty water in real life causes people to float on the surface, but I couldn't think of anything that wasn't really covered by the Soul Sand bubble column already. But I'd love to hear your suggestions. Thanks for reading!

Acquiring enchanted books via villagers should use a template system. Villagers should not be able to trade you any particular book you want by re-rolling their trades. Grian explains why. A version of the villager trade rebalance datapack could be implemented, in which villagers, by default, will only sell you a small non-random subset of the enchanted books found in the game. The rest can only be found as loot in generated structures (e.g. fortune in mineshafts, riptide in ocean ruins, bane of arthropods in spider dungeons, etc.), or in some other unique way that requires the player to actually play the game (e.g. soul speed from piglin bartering, luck of the sea from fishing). However, this would make a lot of enchantments nonrenewable. This is where the template system comes in. If you find an enchanted book not sold by villagers, then a master-level villager will offer to replicate that book for you. This way, you have a sense of making permanent progress in your world as you play, and gives adventuring a better long-term reward. This suggestion is intended to remove the tedium of re-rolling villager trades and replace it with exploring structures and engaging with the game's wide array of other mechanics.

New Minecraft redstone block idea/suggestion: 4-way Itemizer Placed perpendicular to your view, it ingests up to 4 adjacent blocks into internal GUI slots (without dropping them as items) and redeploys them with redstone logic. It can replace laggy flying-machine arrays with compact mechanical magic. The two sides not used for block intake (front and back) handle redstone details. Power levels directly control behavior: •Strength 1 = pulls 1 block (starting left) •Strength >1 = pulls blocks in a circular pattern until power is out •Strength 4 = pulls all 4 blocks •Continuous strength = circular pull/push For example, a redstone power level of 3 pulls the left, top, and right blocks leaving the bottom open. This allows a hopper to sit directly underneath to process blocks straight from the Itemizer. If it can’t ingest any more blocks due to empty space nearby (or being full), but still being powered, it redeploys what it's holding. In short, it’s a compact block buffer and mechanical shift-register for true lag-free vanilla tech builds. This block can allow builds to be reoriented without harm, tree farms to be more compact, more advanced piston doors, and other modular redstone mechanics.

Climbing/Mantling Mechanic TL;DR: After jumping and near a ledge that is more than one blocks high from the ground, players should be able to climb up. One of Minecraft’s greatest strengths is the freedom to explore and adventure through its world. I think a simple climbing/mantling mechanic could make exploration feel smoother and more dynamic without changing the core movement system too much. It is like real life mountain climbing/hiking, we see adventurers use their arms to climb up 2 meter tall ledges after jumping. For example, after jumping toward a ledge, players could have a choice to grab onto and mantle over blocks that are up to 2 blocks high. The mechanic could work similarly to the mantling systems in games like Destiny 2 or Halo Infinite, where the player pulls themselves over a ledge after jumping if they are in contact with the ledge. This could make traversing mountains, caves, ruins, and uneven terrain feel less awkward (block jumping), while still keeping Minecraft’s movement simple and intuitive.

Controversial opinion: The Creaking should appear rarely in any Overworld biome (not limited to the Pale Garden). I feel the Creaking would have worked better if it appeared occasionally in any forest biome, rather than being limited solely to the Pale Garden. This way, the mob's "Creaking Heart" could spawn in any naturally generated tree—much like bee nests (and not just in player-planted trees)—though with the caveat that a heart generated in a non-Pale Garden tree wouldn't produce resin (as that material is exclusive to the Pale Garden biome). As for the design, these variations would simply need to feature colors matching the bark of the tree where the Creaking spawned. It is a real shame that such a unique mob with such cool behavior is confined to a single biome that is both quite rare to find and easy to avoid. I apologize for any writing errors; English is not my native language.

Dwarf Villagers I have made a post about this before, but since it was too long and had too many useless details, I deleted that post and I also added here some more important info. When I say example only, I literally mean it as an example, no need to comment on that. Appearance: Dwarf villagers are smaller than normal villagers, due to them being dwarfs and spawning in caves, where a smaller height is an advantage for them (comparison shown on last image). They have currently 5 professions: 1. Builder (pretty clear which image with bob the builder being on it) 2. Miner (image 2-3) 3. Assayer (image 4) 4. Unemployed (image 5) 5. Wanderer (no image) What they do, will be explained later on. Then they have 7 biomes: 1. Stone (shown in the images) 2. Deepslate 3. Lush cave 4. Sulfur cave 5. Ice caves (when they come out) 6. Lava caves 7. Dripstone caves The way the biome textures and the profession textures will be added is the same (excluding wanderer): They all have the base texture Then the biome texture And lastly the profession texture will be added on top Trading: Miner: The miner will wander in the caves about 50-75 blocks away, depending on the biome. It will only mine emeralds if it sees any (and through walls, though a limited distance of 2 blocks away, maybe even 1) it will mine it. You can trade with it, by giving it emeralds and the ore you want it to find, e.g. raw copper. It will then look for copper and give you maybe 2 pieces more. Now, I have had a lot of people that said this system is too op, it will be balanced, how exactly? I can't tell you, since I haven't gotten to testing this guy out. But, the miner will never have +100'000'000 speed or something, coding this is anyways limited, so it can't find your ores in less than 5 mins, if it even finds it. It will be accompanied by the builder, which will place torches every now and then. The miner can also fight back until half health, in which it fleas. (Yes, it will fight the player too.) Builder: The builder will carry a torch in his hand. It accompanies the miner and the assayer on it's journeys to find ores. It places torches to lighten up the area and prevent enemies from spawning. Assayer: The assayer will inspect ores and hint the miner to ores, since it can see through 3-5 blocks in a wall. It also accompanies the miner. What you can trade with it is unclear yet, as I'm out of ideas, if you know any, please write. Wanderer: He is basically the same as a normal wanderer and will instead of selling you basically useless items, actually sell life saving items (planks, torches, pickaxe etc). Cave Village: The cave village is where the miners live and where they come back at low health to heal. Depending on the biome, the cave village will generate differently. In stone and deepslate caves they will generate completely like mineshafts (or at least a little bit) in which they don't add anything, instead make space for the stuff to be added. However, for more open caves (such as lush caves) they will generate much more openly and only partly generate by making room. If there are any questions please write, I'm mostly looking for ideas though. Thanks for reading, have a nice day :]

The Mist: a new ambience effect for the Pale Garde The Pale Garden is an interesting biome with its "safe in day, leave by night" gameplay with the Creaking and Creaking Hearts (altough unfortunately it can't live up much to it due to how rarely the spawn). However, to really enable such gameplay, there must be a reason to remain in the Garden at night, which it currently lacks (Open Eyeblossoms are just flowers) At least to me, the Pale Garden seems like one of those haunted woods that can be found within many games, where the player can get lost if they aren't careful, and I think it's something that was supposed to happen: the Pale Garden is very dense, so it prevents the player from looking up to the sky to see where the Sun is. Unfortunately, since it requires a high Weirdness value to spawn, it always spawns on top of hills, so one can simply look at the side to measure the time, so leaving the Garden in time is trivial. Also, since most of the time the biomes is rather small, there isn't much room to get lost. To improve on this side of the gameplay, I propose a new ambience effect, similar to what Darkness does in the Deep Dark: the Mist effect. The Mist effect would be given for 10 minutes to all players who come within 50 blocks of the Creaking Heart, in a similar fashion to what the Elder Guardian does, but without the jumpscare. Players affected by the effect, in the span of 10 seconds will have their render distance reduced to a maximum of 4 (visually), while anything beyond will be obscured by a heavy fog; however, anything that glows, such as Enderman and Spider's Eyes, will still be visible in the distance, as also anything affected by the glowing effect (so the player can see in the distance Open Eyeblossoms and Creakings) This will make it much more difficult to navigate the biome once in the depths of it, since the player will have to remember the road they did when entering, possibly wasting their time if the terrain is rough, allowing night to fall and the Creaking to spawn. I think this would make Pale Gardens more interesting to traverse by adding an additional challenge while playing on the biome's "safe at day, leave by night" gameplay. EDIT: this would only work with naturally generated ones
